svg.desc: Banner for a paper on when faster environmental change can only lower the long-run growth rate of a population spread over patches with fixed migration. Left: three patches in a one-way migration loop, 1 to 2 to 3 and back to 1; patches 1 and 2 are forced by waves a quarter period apart, with patch 2 peaking a quarter period before patch 1. Middle: the exact leading-order long-run growth rate, per epsilon squared of forcing, against the speed of environmental change omega from 0 to 4. For this phase order (gold) the curve rises from the slow limit 1/9 to a maximum of about 0.143 at an intermediate speed near omega 0.84, then falls to the fast limit 0. For the opposite order (blue) the curve only falls. Right: the dividing line. With detailed balance, meaning no net flow around any loop of patches, faster change never raises growth; with any circulation, as on this loop, some weak two-patch forcing peaks at an intermediate speed. The certificate computed from migration alone is d12 = 1/9, not zero, here. Gains are of order epsilon squared.
svg.text: Can faster environmental change ever help a spread-out population grow?
Only if migration circulates: growth always falls with speed exactly when migration satisfies detailed balance
patch 2 peaks a quarter period before patch 1
long-run growth rate (per ε² of forcing)
Any circulation, as on this loop:
Exact leading-order response; gains are O(ε²).
